(a): Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency (IREDA) , being a Central Public Sector 
Enterprise (CPSE), follows the employee categorization prescribed under the Department of 
Public Enterprises (DPE) guidelines. Accordingly, employees are broadly classified as Executives 
(E-0 to E-9 level), Non-Unionised Supervisors (S-1 and S-2 level) and Non-Executives (NE-1 to 
NE-7 (Selection Grade (SG)) level). Further, in IREDA, E -1 to E -9 level are classified under 
Group-A, E-0 level is classified under Group-B, NE-3 to NE-7 (Selection Grade) and S -1to S-2 
level are classified under Group-C, NE-1 & NE-2 level are classified under Group-D. The group-
wise details of sanctioned, filled and vacant posts under Groups A, B, C, and D in IREDA  are 
given at Annexure-I. 
 
(b): In compliance with Deptt. of Personnel and Training ( DoPT) Office Memorandum (OM) 
No.36012/2/96-Estt.(Res) dated 02.07.1997, IREDA is maintaining post-based reservation rosters. 
Also, the reservation rosters are maintained for direct recruitment on all India basis - by open 
competition (SCs – 15%, STs – 7.5%) and otherwise than by open competition (SCs – 16.66%, 
STs – 7.5%). The group-wise details of the currently filled posts, vacant and backlog posts as per 
the reservation norms prescribed for Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) are given 
at Annexure-II. 
 
(c): The group-wise details of the sanctioned posts, employees working in the agency, reserved 
posts and filled posts are given at Annexure-III. 
(d): During the last three years, no separate special recruitment drive was undertaken by IREDA. 
However, while undertaking direct recruitment during this period, the vacant as well as backlog 
reserved posts, wherever applicable to the advertised posts, were duly taken into account in 
accordance with the extant guidelines on reservation. Accordingly, the reservation requirements, 
including backlog vacancies, were advertised along with other regular posts, through the regular 
recruitment process. 
 
(e): IREDA is in compliance with the reservation policy of the Government of India and all 
applicable instructions / guidelines issued by the Department of Personnel & Training (DoPT) 
and other competent authorities from time to time. Accordingly, no separate t ime-bound action 
plan has been formulated, as the prescribed reservation provisions are being implemented on a 
continuous basis in all applicable recruitment and service matters.  
Compliance is regularly monitored through maintenance of reservation rosters, periodic reviews, 
and adherence to extant Government instructions to ensure continued compliance.

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (a) to (e) OF THE LOK SABHA STARRED 
QUESTION NO. *16 REGARDING ‘HUMAN-ANIMAL CONFLICT IN TELANGANA’ BY SHRI 
SURESH KUMAR SHETKAR FOR REPLY ON 20.07.2026 
 
 
(a): The management of wildlife including mitigation of human-animal conflicts is primarily the 
responsibility of the concerned State Government/Union Territory Administration. The State 
Government/UT Administration are the first responders to any conflict situation and they maintain the 
details of the conflict along with the species involved. Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme of 
Integrated Development of Wildlife Habitats an amount of Rs. 323.32 lakhs, Rs. 291.68 lakhs, Rs. 
302.34 lakhs and Rs. 208.67 lakhs have been released to the State of Telangana during the financial 
years 2023-24, 2024-25, 2025-26 & 2026-27 respectively for inter alia management of Human wildlife 
conflict.  
 
(b) to (e): Under the said scheme, activities supported include procurement of early warning systems, 
construction and erection of physical barriers such as solar powered electric fencing, bio-fencing, 
trenches, boundary walls etc. to prevent depredation by wild animals which inter alia includes cattle 
lifting, crop damage, loss of life and property. Rapid Response Teams with community stewards are also 
deployed to mitigate Human-Wildlife Conflict.  
 
The Government of India has assessed the status of human wildlife conflict across the country including 
Telangana especially in context of flagship species such as tigers and elephants wherein during the last 
decade no human deaths due to elephants and only 3 human deaths due to tiger attacks were reported by 
the State of Telangana. Further, granular data in respect of compensation and affected districts is collated 
at level of the State.  
 
Important steps taken by the Government to manage human-wildlife conflicts include the following: 
 
i. Section 11 of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 adequately empowers the State Chief Wild 
Life Wardens to manage wildlife in conflict situations. 
 
ii. The Ministry has issued advisories and guidelines to manage human-wildlife negative 
interactions through interdepartmental coordinated actions besides adherence to SOPs in this 
regard. Use of technological aids are used to strengthen these interventions.  
 
iii. The Ministry has established a Centre of Excellence for Human–Wildlife Conflict Management 
at the Salim Ali Centre for Ornithology and Natural History (SACON), WII–South India Centre, 
Coimbatore, to strengthen the scientific and institutional framework for managing human–
wildlife conflict.  
 
 
Further, the Ministry has enhanced the amount of ex-gratia relief in case of death or permanent 
incapacitation due to wild animal attacks in December 2023 from Rs. 5 lakhs to 10 lakhs under these 
Schemes as per the directions in this regard which is supplemented through relevant schemes of the State

(a) & (b) Drinking water is a State subject and hence, the responsibility of planning, approval, 
implementation, operation and maintenance of drinking water supply schemes, including those under 
the Jal Jeevan Mission, lies with th e respective State/UT Governments. The Government of India 
supports the States by providing technical and financial assistance. 
Since August 2019, Government of India, in partnership with States, is implementing Jal Jeevan 
Mission (JJM)-Har Ghar Jal to enable every rural household in the country to have assured potable 
water through tap connection at a service level of 55 litre per capita per day (LPCD), of prescribed 
quality (BIS:10500), on regular and long-term basis. The Union Cabinet has approved the extension 
of the JJM 2.0 by December, 2028 with an enhanced outlay and a restructured implementation 
framework focusing on structural reforms in rural drinking water supply sector. 
As informed by State Govt. of Andhra Pradesh, out of 1539 habitations in Anak apalli district, 549 
habitations are covered with 55 LPCD (100% tap connection) and the remaining 990 habitations are 
scheduled to be covered by December 2028.  
(c) & (d) The planning, design, approval, implementation and day-to-day operation and maintenance 
(O&M) of piped water supply schemes, including the granular tracking of service delivery at the 
individual habitation level, are the responsibilities of the respective State/UT Governments  level 
only, not maintained by national level.  
As reported by the State Government of Chhattisgarh, 1,816 habitations in 33 districts covered under 
JJM but receiving less than fifty -five LPCD of drinking water supply since 2023.  Also, the State 
Government of Chhattisgarh has reported that Since 2023, 471 habitations across five districts have 
been receiving a supply of drinking water almost daily. The district-wise details submitted by the 
State is at Annexure-I.

(a) whether the Union Government provides financial assistance for the development of Integrated 
Tribal Development Agency (ITDA) areas under various schemes, if so, the details thereof;  
(b) the funds allocated, released and utilised under such schemes during the last five years, State-wise,

(c) whether the Government has undertaken any assessment of the implementation and developmental 
outcomes of Central interventions in ITDA areas, if so, the key findings thereof;  
(d) the measures taken to strengthen infrastructure, education, healthcare, livelihoods and skill 
development in ITDA areas; and  
(e) whether any proposals from States/UTs relating to the creation, reorganisation or expansion of ITDA

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (a) TO (e) OF THE LOK SABHA 
STARRED QUESTION NO. 168 FOR 30.07.2026 ASKED BY SHRI TANGELLA UDAY 
SRINIVAS AND SHRI APPALANAIDU KALISETTI, HON’BLE MEMBERS OF 
PARLIAMENT REGARDING DEVELOPMENT OF AREAS UNDER INTEGRATED TRIBAL 
DEVELOPMENT AGENCY 
 
(a) The Union Government supports development in ITDA/ITDP areas through various schemes and 
programmes of the Ministry of Tribal Affairs and other sectoral Ministries. Assistance is provided, inter 
alia, under Grants under Article 275(1) of the Constitution, Pradhan Mantri Adi Adarsh Gram Yojana/State 
Tribal Sub-Plan support, PM-JANMAN, Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (DA-JGUA), 
Eklavya Model Residential Schools, PM-JANMAN, scholarship schemes and tribal livelihood 
programmes. Grants under Article 275(1) are provided to bridge critical gaps in sectors such as education, 
health, agriculture and infrastructure. ITDAs/ITDPs function as important field-level institutions for 
convergence and implementation of these interventions.  
 
(b) Funds under the aforesaid schemes are generally allocated and released State-wise and scheme-wise, 
and not separately for each ITDA/ITDP area. Releases are made on the basis of approved proposals, 
availability of funds, utilisation certificates and compliance with scheme guidelines. The State-wise details 
of funds released during the last five years, including for Andhra Pradesh is at Annexure-I.  
 
(c) The implementation of Central interventions is reviewed regularly through meetings with States/UTs, 
field visits, scheme dashboards, physical and financial progress reports and outcome-based monitoring. 
Further, a National Conclave on Strengthening of ITDAs and ITDPs was organised on 3 June, 2026 to 
assess institutional capacity, convergence, planning and last-mile service delivery. The deliberations 
highlighted the need for stronger staffing, integrated planning, reliable data systems, community 
participation, improved convergence with line departments and greater functional and financial 
empowerment of ITDAs/ITDPs.  
 
(d) The Government is implementing a convergence-based approach in ITDA areas covering: 
(i) Roads, housing, drinking water, electricity, mobile connectivity and other basic infrastructure under 
DA-JGUA, PM-JANMAN and schemes of the concerned line Ministries; 
(ii) Establishment and strengthening of Eklavya Model Residential Schools, hostels, scholarships and other 
educational facilities; 
(iii) Healthcare interventions, including mobile medical units, health screening, maternal and child 
healthcare and the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission; 
(iv) Promotion of agriculture, horticulture, minor forest produce, Van Dhan Vikas Kendras, tribal 
enterprises and market linkages; and 
(v) Skill development, capacity building and livelihood training through convergence with the concerned 
Ministries and State Governments. 
 
(e) Creation, reorganization or expansion of ITDAs/ITDPs is considered on the basis of proposals 
received from the respective State Government/UT Administration and their conformity with the 
prescribed criteria.

STATEMENT 
 
STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS  (a) TO ( f) OF THE 
LOK SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 169 FOR ANSWER ON 30TH 
JULY, 20 26, ASKED BY SHRI MANISH TEWARI  AND SMT. SAJDA 
AHMED REGARDING INFRASTRUCTURE FOR PEDESTRIANS.

(a) to (f)  Government in Ministry of Road Transport & Highways 
regulates the motor vehicles in accordance with the provision s of 
the Motor Vehicles Act and is responsible for development, 
operation and maintenance of National Highways (NHs). Sub-section 
(1A) of section 138 of the Motor Vehicles Act empowers the State 
Governments for making rules for the purposes of regulating 
activities and access of pedestrians to public places a nd National 
Highways. Further, sub -section (2) of s ection 138 provides further 
rule making powers to State Governments for prohibiting use of 
footpaths or pavements by motor vehicles and prevention of da nger, 
injury or annoyance to the public. 
  
As far as pedestrian infrastructure on National Highways is 
concerned, comprehensive guidelines have been published by 
Indian Roads Congress (IRC) viz. IRC:103 -2022 “Guidelines for 
Pedestrian Facilities”. Accordin gly, pedestrian infrastructure such 
as pedestrian underpasses, foot -over bridges, pedestrian crossings, 
footpaths, etc. are integral part of all National Highway projects 
wherever required based upon detailed planning and assessment, 
and are provided as pe r site requirements, either as part of 
improvement works or as stand -alone projects based on audit, to 
ensure seamless movement of the pedestrians. Further, regular 
safety audits are also conducted on all National Highways (NHs) at 
design, construction, an d pre -opening stage of National Highway 
projects as well as on existing NHs for ensuring seamless 
pedestrian infrastructure. IRC guidelines entail “universal 
accessibility” as one of the key principles with regard to pedestrian 
infrastructure. 
  
In accorda nce with the Rule 166 of Central Motor Vehicle Rules, 
1989, the design, construction and maintenance of roads other than 
National Highways shall be in accordance with the standards and 
specifications of the Indian Road Congress as may be applicable, or 

any other instructions or guidelines issued by the State Government 
from time to time. 
  
Government in Ministry of Road Transport & Highways provides 
budgetary support for National Highway projects which includes 
several components including pedestrian infras tructure, wherever 
required, based upon detailed planning and assessment. 
  
The details of fatalities on all roads and pedestrian fatalities 
reported on NHs during the last five years are annexed.

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PART (a) TO (f) OF LOK 
SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 17 BY PROF. VARSHA EKNATH 
GAIKWAD AND SHRI SANJAY DINA PATIL DUE FOR REPLY ON 
20.07.2026 REGARDING "DISBURSEMENT OF INCENTIVES UNDER 
PM-VBRY" 
 
(a) to (f): The Government, on 1 July 2025, approved the 
Employment Linked Incentive (ELI) Scheme, titled the Pradhan 
Mantri Viksit Bharat Rojgar Yojana (PMVBRY), to promote 
employment generation, enhance employability, and strengthen 
social security across all sectors including MSMEs and rural 
enterprises, with a particular focus on the manufacturing sector.  
 
  The scheme aims to incentivise creation of more than 3.5 
Crore jobs all across the country, over a period of 2 years including 
the state of Maharashtra. The scheme comprises of two parts i.e. 
Part A and Part B and focuses on providing support to both 
employees and employers by way of incentives. The scheme 
provides for incentives for 1.92 crore eligible First time employees 
under Part A. Incentive for creation of approximately 2.59 crore 
additional jobs to employers is provided for under Part B of the 
scheme. The Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) is the 
implementing agency for the scheme. 
 
  Prime Minister disbursed incentives worth around ₹2,400 
crore under the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana (PM -
VBRY) at a special programme held on 19 June 20 26 at New Delhi. 
As part of the nationwide outreach effort, PM-VBRY events were also 
organised simultaneously at around 200 locations across the 
country.  
 
  The PMVBRY is a demand-driven scheme. For the State of 
Maharashtra, including Mumbai, under part A, incentive amount of 
Rs 149.41 crore has disbursed to 2.49 lakh first timer employees; and 
under Part B, incentive amount of Rs 435.92 cr has been disbursed 
to 12,701 beneficiary establishments.  
 
  The scheme and its provisions have been widely 
disseminated through extensive outreach efforts across the country. 
EPFO has undertaken awareness and stakeholder outreach 
programmes, including monthly Nidhi Aapke Ni kat (NAN) 
programmes, SMS/email and digital communication campaigns etc. 
to facilitate timely registration and seamless transfer of benefits.  

  A dedicated portal (pmvbry.epfindia.gov.in) has been 
developed to facilitate all scheme -related processes and f or real -
time monitoring of beneficiaries and sector -wise progress. Detailed 
Scheme Guidelines, Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), and 
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) have been made available on 
this portal for ease of understanding.

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO THE PARTS OF (a) to (e) OF LOK SABHA 
STARRED QUESTION NO. *170 FOR ANSWER ON 30.07.2026. 
 
(a): Under the Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI), which was 
in operation upto  September, 2022, 34 clusters have been approved in Rajasthan. Out of these, 25 
clusters are functional and 09 clusters are in progress. The district -wise (including Tonk and Sawai 
Madhopur) number of approved, functional and in -progress clusters in Rajast han are placed at 
Annexure-I. 
 
(b): The total committed Government of India (GoI) assistance for 34 approved clusters in 
Rajasthan is Rs. 93.00 crore, out of which Rs. 78.95 crore has been released and utilized. These 
clusters are benefiting 18,209 artisans, comprising 9,715 male artisans and 8,494 female artisans.  
 
(c): Under the SFURTI Scheme, three clusters have been approved in the Tonk-Sawai Madhopur 
Lok Sabha Constituency, for carpet weaving, handicrafts and beekeeping/honey processing. 
However, no proposal related to stone carving and handloom cluster has been received under the 
Micro and Small Enterprises Cluster Development Programme (MSE -CDP)for the Tonk–Sawai 
Madhopur Lok Sabha Constituency. 
 
(d): As per the Scheme Guidelines, the performance and sustainability of SFURTI clusters, 
including indicators relating to artisans' livelihoods and income generation, are monitored through a 
multi-tier mechanism inv olving the Implementing Agency (IA), Technical Agency (TA), Nodal 
Agency (NA) and the Ministry. The monitoring mechanism includes periodic review meetings, field 
visits, monitoring of production and sales, utilisation of Common Facility Centres (CFCs), mar ket 
linkages, and audited reports, along with review of cluster-level data relating to production, sales and 
other operational parameters to assess cluster performance and sustainability. 
 
(e): Wherever gaps or shortfalls are identified, corrective measures are  undertaken through 
strengthened monitoring, capacity -building and visits, improved utilisation of CFCs, enhanced 
market linkages through participation in fairs, exhibitions and technical handholding, wherever 
feasible, to improve artisans' income-generating opportunities and ensure long-term sustainability of 
the clusters.

IMPACT OF RISING ELECTRICIT Y DEMAND IN PUNJAB  ASKED BY DR. AMAR

*********** 
(a) :  The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) assesses the country's electricity 
requirement and peak demand on a year-on-year basis at the national, regional, 
State, and Union Territory (UT) levels.  The details of month -wise energy 
requirement and peak demand of the State of Punjab for the period April to 
September during the last five years and current year (upto June, 2026) is given 
at Annexure-I. The electricity demand of Punjab increases during p addy 
transplantation season of June to September months every year. 
 
Further, with a view to ensure generation capacity remains ahead of 
projected peak demand, all the States including Punjab, in consultation with 
CEA, have prepared their “Resource Adequac y Plans (RAPs)”, which are 
dynamic 10-year rolling plans and includes power generation as well as power 
procurement planning. Accordingly, assessed energy requirement and peak 
demand of the Punjab from FY 2026-27 to 2031-32 is given at Annexure-II. 
 
(b) :  Government of India has taken the following measures for strengthening 
the transmission and distribution infrastructure, improving grid reliability & 
integrating renewable energy in the country including the state of Punjab: 
 
(i) Capacity addition from non-fossil Sources: Thrust is on capacity addition 
from non-fossil sources, which now exceeds 54% of the total installed 
electricity generation capacity. Further, Government has planned to 
achieve 500 GW of non-fossil fuel based installed generation capacity by 
2030. As per the National Generation Adequacy Plan prepared by CEA in 
March 2026, the non -fossil fuel based installed capacity is likely to 
increase to 786 GW by 2035-36.   
 
(ii) Capacity addition from Conventional Sources: It is projected to increase 
the insta lled capacity of coal -based plants to 315 GW by 2035 -36. 
Keeping in view energy security, no new imported coal -based power 
plants have been planned. 
 
(iii)  Nuclear power has huge potential to ensure long term energy security 
and is vital for India’s clean energy transition towards Net Zero by 2070. 
It is a clean and environment friendly source of base load power. The 
lifecycle emissions of nuclear power are comparable to those of 
renewables like hydro and wind.  Government of India has set an 
ambitious target of 100 GW nuclear power capacity by 2047. 
 
 

(iv)  Energy Storage Systems are being encouraged. Roadmap to 100 GW of 
Hydro Pumped Storage Projects by 2035 -36 has been prepared. As per 
the National Generation Adequacy Plan prepared by CEA in March 2026, 
the likely BESS installed capacity and PSP installed capacity in 2035-36 
is 80 GW and 94 GW respectively. 
 
(v) 100% Inter State Transmission System (ISTS) charges have been waived 
for inter -state sale of solar and wind power for projects to be 
commissioned by 30th June 2025 (with waiver tapering off 25% annually 
till June 2028), for co-located BESS projects commissioned by June 2028, 
for Hydro PSP projects where construction work awarded by June 2028, 
for Green Hydrogen Projects commissioned till December 2030 and for 
offshore wind projects commissioned till December 2032. 
 
(vi) Standard Bidding Guidelines for tariff based competitive bidding process 
for procurement of Power from Grid Connected Solar, Wind, Wind -Solar 
Hybrid and Firm & Dispatchable RE (FDRE)

ON 30.07.2026 REGARDING "AWARENESS REGARDING PASSENGER

(a): Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) has issued the P assenger Charter to 
ensure that air travellers are aware of their rights and responsibilities. The 
Charter outlines passengers' rights in situations such as flight delays, flight 
cancellations, denied boarding due to overbooking, ticket refunds, flight 
diversions, medical emergencies and lost, delayed or damaged baggage.  
 
To enhance passenger awareness, all airports are required to display a QR code 
linking to the Passenger Charter under the heading "Know Your Rights When 
You Fly" at check -in counters, boa rding gates and other prominent locations 
within airport terminals. In addition, all airlines have been instructed to share 
the link to the Passenger Charter at the time of ticket booking through digital 
messages or by displaying it on the ticket itself. 
 
(b): The AirSewa portal, an initiative by MoCA, enables grievance redressal in 
a time-bound manner and provides a one -stop solution for hassle-free air travel. 
It allows passengers to submit and track grievances related to various 
stakeholders such as Ai rlines, Airports, Security, DGCA, Customs, 
Immigration, BCAS under various grievance categories including Baggage 
Claim. 
 
Further, the Ministry has established a permanent, 24*7 Passenger Assistance 
Control Room (PACR) to enhance passenger-centric governance. This initiative 
integrates MoCA, DGCA, AAI and airlines for real -time monitoring of flight 
disruptions, baggage issues and refunds, aiming to accelerate grievance 
redressal and improve the overall travel experience. 
 
The total grievances received d uring the period from 01.01.2026 to 30.06.2026 
were 64,641, of which 64,546 have been resolved, resulting in resolution rate of 
99.85%. 
 
(c): Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has issued various passenger 
centric Civil Aviation Requirements (C ARs), to ensure adequate protection for 
air travellers and safeguard the interests of the travelling public. To monitor 
compliance with the provisions of the relevant CAR by the airline, DGCA 

conducts surveillance inspections and spot checks at airports across the country. 
In case of non -compliance, enforcement action, including imposition of 
financial penalty, is taken by DGCA. 
 
(d): Passenger traffic at airports vary depending on several factors such as 
seasonal demand, festivals, holidays, and airline schedules. During peak travel 
periods, higher passenger footfall may be observed at some airports which could 
lead to temporary congestion. However, airport operators continuously monitor 
passenger traffic and take necessary operational measures to ensure smooth 
passenger facilitation and efficient airport operations. 
 
(e): In order to ensure appropriate protection for the air travellers, DGCA has 
issued following passenger centric regulations/circulars to safeguard the interest 
of the travelling public: 
(i) Carriage by Air of Persons with Disability and/ or Persons with Reduced 
Mobility (CAR Section 3, Series M, Part I). 
(ii) Facilities to be provided to passengers by airlines due to denied boarding, 
cancellation of flights and delays in flights (CAR Section 3, Series M, Part IV).

LOK SABHA 
STARRED QUESTION NO. 173 
TO BE ANSWERED ON JULY 30, 2026 
 
HOUSES UNDER PMAY - U 2.0 IN DUMKA, JHARKHAND 
 
 
NO. 173 SHRI NALIN SOREN:  
 
Will the Minister of HOUSING AND URBAN AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 
(a) whether the Government has sanctioned houses under Pradhan 
Mantri Awas Yojana - Urban 2.0 (PMAY-U 2.0) in Dumka Municipal 
Council area of Jharkhand; 
(b) if so, the number of houses sanctioned,  under construction and 
completed so far under the said yojana; 
(c) the amount of central assistance sanctioned and released so far 
to Dumka Municipal Council under the said yojana; and 
(d) whether the Government proposes to take any special steps to 
provide housing to eligible beneficiaries at the earliest and settle 
the pending cases in a time- bound manner in Dumka Municipal 
Council and if so, the details thereof? 
 
ANSWER 
THE MINISTER OF HOUSING AND URBAN AFFAIRS 
(SHRI MANOHAR LAL) 
 
(a) to (d): A statement is laid on the Table of the House.  
 
 
 
 
 
 

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN THE LOK SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 
173* ( 13TH POSITION) DUE FOR ANSWER ON 30.07.2026 REGARDING 
“HOUSES UNDER PMAY-U 2.0 IN DUMKA, JHARKHAND” 
 
(a) to (c):    Based on the project proposals received from the State 
Government of Jharkhand, a total of 14,187 houses have been sanctioned 
with the Central Assistance of ₹ 211.57 crore under Pradhan Mantri Awas 
Yojana – Urban 2.0 (PMAY-U 2.0). Out of this, a meagre figure of 118 houses 
are sanctioned in Dumka Municipal Council with the approved Central 
Assistance of ₹1.76 crore. The first instalment of 40% of approved Central 
Assistance against the approved houses in Dumka Municipal Council, i.e. 
₹70.2 lakh will be given to state government through mother sanction under 
SNA-SPARSH within a month. The progress of the scheme can also be 
accessed on the PMAY -U dashboard ( https://dashboard.pmay-urban.gov.in). 
 
 
(d):  PMAY-U 2.0 adopts a demand driven approach and no target has been 
fixed by the Government. States/ Union Territories ( UTs) assess the 
requirement through their Urban Local Bodies (ULBs)/Implementing Agencies 
in their respective jurisdictions. Eligible citizens apply through Unified Web 
Portal of PMAY-U 2.0 with all details on the portal. States/UTs/ULBs validate 
the beneficiaries as per the eligibility criteria of the scheme guidelines and 
selection/scrutiny of beneficiary lists are done by the States/UTs. The 
Scheme Guidelines and Unified Web Portal for submitting the online 
applications can be accessed through https://pmay -urban.gov.in. Based on 
the demand survey and selection of beneficiaries, the project proposals are 
prepared and approved by the State Level Sanctioning and Monitoring 
Committee (SLSMC) headed by the Chief Secretary of States/UTs for further 
consideration of release of Central Assistance by the Central Sanctioning and 
Monitoring Committee (CSMC).  However, the Government of Jharkhand 
decided to implement PMAY -U 2.0 only on 06.05.2026. No project proposal 
from Government of Jharkhand including Dumka is pending with the Ministry.

Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION 
be pleased to state:- 
(a) the details of helicopter services sanctioned under the UDAN Helicopter 
Scheme in Odisha during the period from 2020-21 to 2025-26; 
(b) the criteria adopted for the selection of districts under the UDAN Helicopter 
Scheme; 
(c) whether the Government has examined the feasibility of introducing helicopter 
connectivity for Balangir and Subarnapur in view of their distance from major 
airports and healthcare facilities and if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the measures taken by the Gover nment to strengthen emergency medical 
evacuation and disaster response through helicopter connectivity in western 
Odisha?

Minister of CIVIL AVIATION      (Shri Kinjarapu Rammohan Naidu)

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (A) TO (D) IN RESPECT 
OF LOK SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 175 FOR ANSWER ON 
30.07.2026 REGARDING "UDAN HELICOPTER SCHEME IN ODISHA" 
ASKED BY SMT SANGEETA KUMARI SINGH DEO. 
 
(a) to (d):  Helicopter operations under  the UDAN Scheme were introduced from 
the 2nd round of bidding in 2017 to enhance regional air connectivity in Priority 
Areas, namely Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, the North -
Eastern States, Andaman & Nicobar Islands, and Lakshadweep Islan ds. Under the 
UDAN 5.1 round of bidding in 2023, the eligibility criteria was revised to allow 
helicopter operations provided that at least one origin or destination is a heliport 
and one of the locations lies in a Priority Area. No airline submitted bids 
connecting the helipads in Odisha with locations that lie within the Priority Areas. 
 
The next phase of the UDAN Scheme, launched on 04.07.2026, expands helicopter 
connectivity by envisaging the development of 200 modern helipads in 
Aspirational Districts, including in the State of Odisha and Priority Area districts 
where no heliport or airport is operational or under development, which will 
facilitate improved access for passenger connectivity as well as support emergency 
medical evacuation, disaster res ponse and relief operations in remote and 
underserved areas.

framework for project selection, funding pattern and the progress 
achieved during the Financial Year 2025- 26, particularly in Dahod Lok

REGARDING “IMPLEMENTATION OF URBAN CHALLENGE FUND” 
(a) to (d): The Urban Challenge Fund (UCF) scheme has been 
operationalized with the launch of Operational Guidelines for UCF on 15th 
April, 2026. So far, 33 projects have been approved/ accorded in- principle 
approval. The State- wise details are given in Annexure. No proposal has 
been received from Gujarat State for Dahod Lok Sabha Constituency.  
 
The UCF provides a total Central Assistance of ₹1 lakh crore over the 
Mission period. Under UCF, Central Assistance is limited to 25 per cent of 
the cost of bankable projects, with the stipulation that at least 50 per cent 
of the project cost shall be fina nced through market -based sources, 
including municipal bonds, bank loans and Public- Private Partnerships 
(PPPs). The remaining project cost is to be met by the concerned 
State/UT/ULB. 
 
All Cities are eligible to participate under UCF . Chapter 7 of the operational 
guidelines includes details regarding the Project Appraisal and Challenge 
Framework including mandatory eligibility requirements, overall project 
flow/ implementation framework,  and project evaluation process for 
appraisal and selection of projects. The list of admissible projects under 
UCF are given under chapter 5 of the operational guidelines. The scheme 
guidelines are in public domain and may be accessed at  
https://www.mohua.gov.in/static/uploads/2026/04/7950afb9b2d5cb773ba3d
6c64bde9726.pdf  
 
UCF supports the development and strengthening of urban infrastructure 
through implementation of transformative and impactful projects under 
three verticals namely ‘Cities as Growth Hubs’, ‘Creative Redevelopment of 
Cities’ and ‘Water and Sanitation’.

DELAY IN DISBURSEMENT OF FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE UNDER PMEGP 
 
*177.  SHRI SHREYAS M PATEL:  
 
Will the Minister of MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES be pleased to state: 
 
(a) whether the Government is aware of delays in the sanction and disbursement of financial  
assistance under the Prime Minister's Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) in various  
States, including Karnataka and if so, the details thereof; 
 
(b) the number of PMEGP applications   received, sanctioned, pending, rejected  and disbursed 
during the last five years, State-wise and year-wise; 
 
(c) the average time taken for processing applications, sanctioni ng projects,  releasing margin  
money subsidy and disbursing loans under PMEGP; 
 
(d) the major reasons for delays in sanction and disbursement of assistance under  PMEGP and 
the corrective measures taken by the Government to address these issues; and 
 
(e) whether the Government proposes to simplify the approval process, strengthen  coordination 
with banks, introduce timelines for disposal of applications and  ensure timely release of financial 
assistance to eligible beneficiaries and if so, the details thereof? 
 
ANSWER 
 
MINISTER OF MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES 
(SHRI JITAN RAM MANJHI) 
 
(a) to (e): A statement is laid on the table of the House. 
  

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (a) TO (e) OF THE LOK SABHA 
STARRED QUESTION No. 177 FOR ANSWER ON 30.07.2026 
 
(a):  The time taken for sanction of loans and disbursement of Margin Money subsidy under 
PMEGP in various States, including Karnataka, depends upon fulfillment of application process 
with supporting documents, appraisal of project viability and credit decision by the financing banks, 
deposit of own contribution and completion of Entrepreneurship Development Programme (EDP) 
training by the prospective beneficiaries and submission of Margin Money subsidy claims by 
financing banks.  
 
(b):  State-wise and year -wise details of number of applications received, sanctioned, pending 
and rejected by Banks; and number of applications for which MM Subsidy has been disbursed 
during the last five years under PMEGP is given at Annexure I.   
 
(c):  The average time taken for processing PMEGP applications by Implementing Agencies, 
sanction of loan by Banks and release of Margin Money (MM)subsidy by KVIC during the last five 
years is 58, 70 and 84 days, respectively.  
 
(d) and (e):  The Government closely monitors  the implementation of the Prime Minister’s 
Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP), including time taken in sanction and disbursement 
of financial assistance in the form of MM subsidy across the country, including Karnataka.  
 
Corrective Measures undertak en by the Government to streamline the approval process, 
strengthen coordination with financing banks for loan sanction, expedite disposal of applications 
and timely release of MM subsidy under PMEGP include the following: 
 
i. Pending applications and MM subs idy claims are regularly monitored and reviewed by the 
Government and financing banks through Quarterly Bankers’ Meetings at State and Zonal 
level, State Level Monitoring Committee (SLMC) and District Level Monitoring Committee 
(DLMC) meetings. 
ii. To assist applicants in preparing project proposals, more than 1,000 model Detailed Project 
Reports (DPRs) covering various sectors have been made available on the PMEGP Portal. 
iii. To reduce entry barriers, educational qualification requirements are waived for projects in 
manufacturing sector up to Rs. 10 lakh and in service sector up to Rs. 5 lakh. 
iv. To expedite approvals for small projects, EDP training has been exempted for projects up to 
Rs. 2 lakh. 
v. To provide guidance, facilitate applications and offer real -time assistance to prospective 
entrepreneurs, PMEGP Helpdesks have been established at State level and awareness 
programmes and financial literacy camps are conducted in all States/UTs, including 
aspirational districts, underperforming areas and North-Eastern Region. 
vi. PMEGP Portal developed as an end-to-end digital platform is integrated with financing banks 
through Jan Samarth Portal, streamlining the approval process and with SMS alert to 
applicants at different stages and facilitation of Udyam Registration.

entries.head:
GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
LOK SABHA 
STARRED QUESTION NO. : 178 
 ( TO BE ANSWERED ON THE  30th July 2026 )  
RISING PRICES OF AVIATION TURBINE FUEL  
178.    SHRI JANARDAN MISHRA                     
             SHRI SATISH KUMAR GAUTAM                 
 
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION 
be pleased to state:- 
(a) whether the Government has taken any steps to provide relief to the airlines in view 
of the rising prices of Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) globally and if so, the details thereof; 
 
(b) the details of the projected financial implications of such measures on airport 
operators and other concerned stakeholders; and 
 
(c) the criteria or parameters adopted by the Government for determining the nature  
and extent of relief measures to be provided to domestic airlines? 
ANSWER 
Minister of CIVIL AVIATION      
 (Shri Kinjarapu Rammohan Naidu) 
(a) to (c): A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
****** 
  

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (A) TO ( C) IN 
RESPECT OF LOK SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 178 FOR REPLY 
ON 30.07.2026 REGARDING 'RISING PRICES OF AVIATION TURBINE 
FUEL' ASKED BY SHRI JANARDAN MISHRA AND SHRI SATISH 
KUMAR GAUTAM.   
 
(a) to (c): The Government in consultation with stakeholders has taken 
several measures to support the aviation sector and help keep air travel 
affordable, which include:  
 
(i) For domestic operations, ATF prices were capped at a maximum 
increase of 25% over the 1 March 2026 base price, effective from 1 April 
2026 for the months of April and May 2026, 
(ii) Partial deferment of airport landing and parking charges for domestic 
operations at major airports along with a 25% rebate in such charges at 
Airports Authority of India (AAI) airports, 
(iii) Approval of ECLGS 5.0 with a total corpus of Rs. 18,100 crore, 
including Rs. 5,000 crore earmarked for Indian airlines, to provide liquidity 
support, 
(iv) Reduction of Value Added Tax (VAT) on ATF at Delhi (from 25% to 
7%) and at Maharashtra (from 18% to 7%) for 6 months.  
 
Further, the Government has approved a one-time ATF Price Stabilisation 
Fund (PSF) Scheme with a budgetary support not exceeding Rs. 10,000 
crore as a contingency measure in response to the exceptional sur ge in 
international ATF prices arising from the West Asia crisis, with the 
objective of protecting domestic airlines and ensuring operational stability. 
 
*****

(a):  Implementation of National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 is a continuous process. It 
provides different timelines as well as principles and methodology for its implementation. 
NEP 2020 envisages operationalisation of the entire policy during the decade 2030 –2040, 
following which another comprehensive review will be undertaken. 
 UDISE + provides information on the changes in the Educational Indicators.  As per 
UDISE+ 2025-26 data, the enrolment in the schools has gone up to 24.72 crores.  The Net 
Enrolment Ratio has improved in FY 2025-26 as compared to 2024-25 across Foundational, 
Preparatory, Middle and Secondary stages of schooling.  The Gender Parity Index is 1.0 or 
more across all stages of sch ool showing active participation of girls.  The availability of 
infrastructure facilities like Girls, Boys and CWSN toilets, drinking water, electricity, ramps 
with handrails and aspirational facilities like internet connection, computer availability have 
all registered improvement. The UDISE+ 2025 -26 is available at weblink 
https://udiseplus.gov.in/#/en/page/publications . 
 Department of School Education & Literacy (DoSE&L), Ministry of E ducation, has 
aligned various Centrally Sponsored Schemes, such as Samagra Shiksha, PM Schools for 
Rising India (PM SHRI), Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman (PM POSHAN) Scheme, 
and Understanding Lifelong Learning for All in Society (ULLAS), to facilitate  achievement 
of the goals of NEP 2020 across all levels of school education. 
 Further, education is in the Concurrent List of the Constitution, and the majority of 
schools are under the administrative domain of the respective State and UT Governments. 
Therefore, the primary responsibility for implementation of NEP 2020, in accordance with 
the prescribed norms and standards, rests with the respective State and UT Governments.

schools from State of Karnataka.

(a) to (d): ‘Public Health’ & ‘Hospitals’ are State subjects. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
provides technical and financial support to the States/UTs to strengthen the public healthcare system,
based on the proposals received in the form of Programme Implementation Plans (PIPs) under National
Health Mission (NHM). Approval is accorded to the proposals in the form of Record of Proceedings
(RoPs) as per norms & available resources.
Health Dynamics of India (HDI) is an annual publication, based on healthcare administrative data
reported by States/UTs. Details of availability of health infrastructure including Primary Health Centres
(PHCs), Sub-Health Centres (SHCs), Community Health Centres (CHCs), Sub Divisional Hospitals
(SDHs) and District Hospitals (DHs) and other health units across the country including Maharashtra,
district-wise, may be accessed through the HMIS portal under Publications at the following link of HDI
2023-24:
https://hmis.mohfw.gov.in
Through 1.86 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs), including 13,457 AAMs in Maharashtra and
369 AAMs in Ahilyanagar district, comprehensive primary healthcare is provided by strengthening
Sub-Health Centres (SHCs) and Primary Health Centres (PHCs). These AAMs are required to provide
preventive, promotive, rehabilitative and curative care for an expanded range of services encompassing
reproductive and child healthcare services, Non-communicable diseases, Communicable Diseases,
Elderly and Palliative Care, Mental Health Care, Oral Health, Eye and ENT care and basic emergency
care.
Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM) is a Centrally Sponsored
Scheme (CSS) with certain Central Sector (CS) components, which has been implemented to strengthen
India's public health system through reforms that integrate health service delivery, public health action
and health research, thereby enhancing the capacity of public health systems to effectively respond to
pandemics and other public health emergencies. Total amount of Rs. 1,195.14 crore has been allocated
under PM-ABHIM for the State of Maharashtra for FY 2021-22 to FY 2025-26. Approvals have been
accorded to the State for 36 Integrated District Public Health Laboratories (IPHLs) and 36 Critical Care
Hospital Blocks (CCBs), amounting to Rs. 1086.44 crore including 1 IPHL and 1 CCB in Ahilyanagar
district.
Under Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY), setting up of 22 All India Institutes of
Medical Sciences (AIIMS) has been approved including one AIIMS at Nagpur in Maharashtra, which is
functional. Further, for expansion and strengthening of tertiary healthcare facilities in Maharashtra,
under another component of PMSSY upgradation of six (06) Government Medical Colleges/ Institutes
have been approved by way of construction of Super Specialty Blocks (SSBs) on Centre-State cost

sharing basis: (i) Grant Medical College & Sir JJ Group of Hospitals, Mumbai (ii) Government Medical
College, Nagpur (iii) Govt. Medical College, Aurangabad (iv) Govt. Medical College, Latur (v) Govt.
Medical College, Akola and (vi) Shri Vasantrao Naik Govt. Medical College, Yavatmal.
Under Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for ‘Establishment of new medical colleges attached with
existing district/referral hospitals’, out of 157 medical colleges approved, 02 medical colleges have been
approved in Gondia and Nandurbar district in Maharashtra and are functional.

*184 SHRI BENNY BEHANAN:

Will the MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) the measures taken by the Government after the World Health Organization declared the Ebola Virus
outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC);
(b) the number of individuals screened for Ebola Virus at airports in India between May and July 2026,
State/UT-wise and airport-wise;
(c) the precautionary and preparedness measures taken by the Government to respond to any suspected
or confirmed Ebola Virus Disease cases in the country; and
(d) whether the Government restricted the entry of travellers from countries affected by the Ebola
outbreak into India, if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
(SHRI JAGAT PRAKASH NADDA)
(a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.

STATEMENTREFERRED TO IN REPLYTO LOK SABHA
STARRED QUESTION NO. 184* FOR 31TH JULY,2026
(a) to (d): Following the declaration of the Bundibugyo Ebola disease outbreak as a Public Health
Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) by World Health Organization (WHO) and Public Health
Emergency of Continental Security (PHECS) by the Africa Centre for Disease Control and Prevention
(Africa CDC), the Government strengthened surveillance and public health preparedness across the
country in accordance with the temporary recommendations of WHO.
These measures have been undertaken in close coordination with National Centre for Disease
Control, Indian Council for Medical Research, Directorate General Health Services, Ministry of Civil
Aviation, Ministry of Home Affairs, Ministry of External Affairs, Ministry of Ports, Shipping &
Waterways,Department of Biotechnology and other stakeholders.
Enhanced screening and surveillance measures have been instituted at International airports and
other Points of Entry. In addition, advisories and Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) covering
surveillance, screening, quarantine, clinical management, laboratory testing and infection prevention
practices, case reporting have been issued to all States and Union Territories to ensure a coordinated
preparedness and response. As on date no case of Ebola Disease has been reported in the country. The
precautionary and preparedness measures undertaken by the Government are at Annexure 1.
The Government as such has not imposed a blanket restriction on the entry of travellers from
Ebola-affected countries. However, as per SOP for public health preparedness and response to Ebola
disease issued by the Government, all international passengers arriving at Points of Entry are screened
for a history of travel to Ebola disease affected countries namely Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC),
Uganda and South Sudan during the preceding 21 days.
As per the Self Declaration Forms submitted by international passengers including through the
Air Suvidha 2.0 portal, a total of 10,974 passengers coming from the aforesaid countries have been
screened from 23rd May uptil 28th July, 2026. The State/UT-wise and airport-wise details number of
individuals screened for Ebola Virus are at Annexure 2 & 3 respectively.

ANNEXURE 1
Measures undertaken by the Government after the World Health Organization declared the Bundibugyo
Ebola disease outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC);
 Issued detailed Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and operational guidelines covering
surveillance, reporting, Infection Prevention and Control, technical specifications for Personnel
Protective Equipment, laboratory diagnosis, sample transportation, quarantine, isolation and
discharge of cases.
 Identification and operational readiness of designated isolation facilities across States and UTs.
 Expanded laboratory diagnostic capacity through ICMR-NIV ,Pune and additional designated
Biosafety Level-3 laboratories across the country.
 Ensuring availability of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) and other logistics for healthcare
workers throughout the country including Points of Entry.
 Conducted mock drills in designated hospitals across all States/UTs to assess preparedness.
 Capacity building of APHOs, Bureau of Immigration officials, State Surveillance Units across
all states and designated isolation hospitals.

clinical decision support and health service delivery in the country;
(b) if so, the steps taken by the Government for its implementation, including the Government

(c) the measures being taken to promote the adoption of AI-enabled healthcare solutions in Government
health facilities, particularly in rural and underserved regions of the country, Statewise;
(d) whether a regulatory framework has been put in place to ensure ethical, secure and
responsible use of AI in healthcare, including the protection of patient data and transparency in

STATEMENTREFERRED TO IN REPLYTO LOK SABHA
STARRED QUESTION NO. 186* FOR 31TH JULY,2026
(a) to (e) Yes, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has launched the ‘Strategy for AI in
Healthcare’ (SAHI) on 17th February 2026 during the India AI impact summit. SAHI is a national
guidance framework to enable the safe, ethical, evidence-based, responsible and inclusive adoption
of artificial intelligence across India’s healthcare system. SAHI has been developed after extensive
consultation with several major stakeholders of the healthcare ecosystem.
The Ministry of Health has designated All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) Delhi,
Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER) Chandigarh and All India
Institute of Medical Sciences Delhi (AIIMS) Rishikesh as ‘Centres of Excellence (CoE) for artificial
intelligence’. The key objective of AI initiative of ‘centre of excellence’ is to promote development
and use of AI-based solutions in health.
Several AI solutions have been developed. Some of these include the CIinical Decision Support
System (CDSS) on e-Sanjeevani platform to provide symptom based clinical diagnosis and thus to
assist doctors in providing faster and more accurate consultations; Media Disease Surveillance under
Integrated Disease Surveillance Program (IDSP) to enable early detection and monitoring of disease
outbreaks; a Diabetic Retinopathy (DR identification solution) to assist in the timely screening and
diagnosis of vision-threatening eye diseases; AI enabled tools for identifying hotspots for TB,
Leprosy, Malaria, other vector borne diseases etc. for targeted interventions across the country,
including rural & underserved regions; AI-enabled handheld X-rays for TB screening & early
diagnosis through community outreach activities; TB Mukt Bharat App, featuring the AI-powered
Khushi Chatbot that provides medication reminders, treatment guidance, adherence support,
follow-up assistance, and nutritional and psychosocial support for TB patients. These AI solutions
are operational in collaboration with central and state health institutions across the country.
Together, these solutions address multiple aspects of healthcare including disease detection,
diagnostics, clinical decision support and health service delivery. Diabetic Retinopathy identification
solution enables early disease detection and treatment, CDSS supports possible differential diagnosis,
and MDS facilitates early outbreak detection and prompt public health action, while a range of
solutions for detection of TB and other AI health applications support health service delivery.
Further, safeguards for data privacy, consent and AI accountability are ensured by compliance to
various policies and guidelines issued from time to time. These include: Ethical guidelines for
Application of Artificial Intelligence in Biomedical Research and Healthcare by ICMR which
ensures that AI is developed, validated, deployed, and monitored in a manner that protects patients,
promotes public trust, and supports responsible innovation; India AI Governance guidelines by

SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 187 FOR REPLY ON 31.07.2026 
REGARDING “CONTRIBUTION OF INDIA FOR GLOBAL PEACE”. 
India has consistently sup ported the United Nations in strengthening 
international peace and security. This support has been expressed in a 
variety of ways, including its unique contribution to UN peacekeeping 
operations. This contribution is also reflected in India’s membership of  
the UN Security Council on 8 occasions, with the next candidature 
formally announced for 2028 -29. Each tenure has witnessed placing 
issues of Indian interest on the international agenda, the last in 2021 -22 
being maritime security and counter -terrorism. T he six priorities for the 
2028-29 candidature are: (i) A Voice of Global South (ii) Advancing 
Reformed Multilateralism (iii) A Future Ready Peacekeeping (iv) 
Addressing threats posed due to misuse of AI (v) Securing Maritme 
Commons (vi) Countering Terror Financing.   
India is a key contributor to global peace and security, with almost 
3,00,000 peacekeepers serving in more than 50 UN missions. Currently, 
4,200 Indian peacekeepers are deployed in 9 out of 11 active missions, 
working in challenging conditions to promote international peace.  India’s 
engagement in peacekeeping activities is held in high esteem by the UN 

3 
and member states which is illustrated in various citations and awards 
received by our peacekeepers.  
In recent times, issues pertaining to glob al peace have been debated in 
the United Nations as well as other forums. India has firmly advanced its 
view that dialogue and diplomacy are the best means to achieve lasting 
and durable peace. This has been stated in respect of the Ukraine conflict, 
the developments in West Asia as well as hostilities in the Gulf.  
With regard to the challenge of terrorism, India has strongly advocated a 
policy of zero -tolerance and asserted the right of nations to defend 
themselves against terrorism. Since 1996, India has  also called for the 
adoption of a Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism. India 
supports the counter -terrorism mechanisms established by UN Security 
Council Resolutions, including Resolutions 1267 and 1988 and its 
successors related to sancti ons against Al -Qaeda, Islamic State of Iraq 
and Levant (ISIL), and associated entities such as Lashkar-e-Tayyiba (LeT) 
and Jaish-e-Mohammad (JeM). The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), 
as the National Central Bureau for INTERPOL, provides assistance t o 
Indian law enforcement agencies in investigation of cases of terrorism 
and organized crime.  
On cyber -security, India participates in all UN -mandated processes on 
Information and Communication Technology (ICT) security including the 

4 
newly established per manent Global Mechanism on developments in the 
field of ICTs for international security and advancing responsible State 
behaviour in the use of ICTs. India hosted the AI Impact Summit in 
February 2026, where it put forward a human-centric vision of AI – MANAV, 
which stands for Moral and ethical systems; Accountable governance; 
National Sovereignty; Accessible and inclusive; Valid and legitimate 
systems. 
India’s global role has benefited from its effective and purposeful 
multilateral diplomacy. Recent examples of this include election of Indian 
candidates to International Tribunal for the Law of Seas (ITLOS) and Vice-
President of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF).  India’s candidatures 
have received wide support across member states, e.g. election to the  
United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC) for the seventh term (2026-
2028), re-election to the Executive Board of the UNESCO (2025-2029), UN 
Economic and Social Council (2026-2028), Vice Chair 2025 and Chair 2026 
of the Kimberley Process, re -election to Council of the International Civil 
Aviation Organisation (ICAO), Council of the International Maritime 
Organization (IMO), election to the Postal Operations Council (POC) and 
Council of Administration of Universal Postal Union (UPU) 2026-2029.

(a) & (b) Following steps are taken by the Government every season for ensuring 
timely and adequate availability of fertilizers in the country: 
 
(i) Before the commencement of each cropping season, Department of 
Agriculture and Farmers Welfare (DA&FW), in consultation with all the State 
Governments, assesses the State-wise & month-wise requirement of 
fertilizers. On the basis of requirement projected by DA&FW, Department of 
Fertilizers (DoF) allocates adequate quantities of fertilizers to States by issuing 
monthly supply plan and continuously monitors the availability. 
 
(ii) The movement of all major subsidized fertilizers is monitored throughout the 
country by an on-line web-based monitoring system called integrated Fertilizer 
Management System (iFMS). 
 
(iii) The gap between demand (requirement) and production for Urea & other 
fertilizers is met through imports. The import for the season is also finalized 
well in advance to ensure timely availability.  
 
(iv) The State Governments are regularly advised to coordinate with 
manufacturers and importers for streamlining the supplies through timely 
placement of indents. 
 
(v) Regular coordination is done with the Ministry of Railways for giving sufficient 
rakes, priority to fertilizers and for timely evacuation of rakes for States. 
 
(vi) The distribution of fertilizers within the State at district/block level is done by 
the concerned State government.

Statement referred to in reply to parts (a) to (e) in respect of Lok Sabha Starred 
Question No. 190 for reply on 31.07.2026 regarding Rashtriya Chemicals and 
Fertilizers Ltd asked by Thiru Dayanidhi Maran. 
 
(a) to (c): The Board of Directors of Rashtriya Chemicals and Fertilizers (RCF) in its 
500th meeting held on 7th July 2026 has accorded in principle approval on the proposal 
of raising funds amounting to Rs. 1500 crore through a Further Public Offer (FPO) to 
meet ongoing and future capital expenditure. The proposal is under consideration of the 
government. 
 
The capital raised through the proposed FPO is intended to fund balance equity 
infusion in the existing Joint Venture - Talcher Fertilizers Limited (TFL) and to have 
Strategic Joint Venture Investments by collaborating with other stakeholders to support 
India's fertilizer security and reduce dependence on imports.  
     
 (d):      The renewable energy and water management initiatives of RCF are aimed at 
improving operational efficiency, sustainability and resource optimization, while the 
agrochemical initiatives are intended to broaden the product basket and support 
integrated crop nutrition. These initiatives are not expected to adversely affect fertilizer 
production or supply to farmers.  
 
(e):     Decisions regarding establishment or expansion of fertilizer manufacturing 
facilities are taken after due consideration of factors such as regional fertilizer demand, 
availability of raw materials, techno-economic feasibility, financial viability, logistics and 
other locational advantages. Such requirements are assessed periodically to ensure 
efficient fertilizer production and distribution across the country. 
 
The following steps are taken by the Government in every season for ensuring 
timely and adequate supply of fertilizers in the country, including in the State of Tamil 
Nadu: 
 
I. Before the commencement of each cropping season, Department of Agriculture 
and Farmers Welfare (DA&FW), in consultation with all the State Governments, 
assesses the State-wise & month-wise requirement of fertilizers. On the basis of 
requirement projected by DA&FW, Department of Fertilizers (DoF) allocates 
adequate quantities of fertilizers to States by issuing monthly supply plan and 
continuously monitors the availability. 
 
II. The movement of all major subsidized fertilizers is monitored throughout the 
country by an on-line web-based monitoring system called integrated Fertilizer 
Management System (iFMS). 
 
III. The gap between demand (requirement) and production for Urea & other 
fertilizers is met through imports. The import for the season is also finalized well in 
advance to ensure timely availability. 

3 
 
 
 
 
 
 
IV. The State Governments are regularly advised to coordinate with manufacturers 
and importers for streamlining the supplies through timely placement of indents. 
 
V. Regular coordination with the Ministry of Railways is undertaken for giving 
sufficient rakes, priority to fertilizers and for timely evacuation of rakes for States. 
 
VI. The distribution of fertilizers within the State at district level is done by the 
concerned State government.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF AYUSH

STARRED QUESTION NO. 193 
TO BE ANSWERED ON 31.07.2026 
Research and Development Projects under AYURGYAN Scheme 
 
*193. Shri Ravindra Shukla Alias Ravi Kishan: 
          Dr. Sanjay Jaiswal: 
    Will the Minister of AYUSH  
be pleased to state:  
(a) the details of the progress of the 16 ongoing Research and Development (R&D) projects 
under the AYURGYAN Scheme in the country, State/UT-wise, including Odisha, particularly 
in the Keonjhar Parliamentary constituency; 
(b) the details of the operational status of the Ayurveda Biology Integrated Health Research 
(ABIHR) component; 
(c) the details and the projected timeline for setting up the three new All lndia Institutes of 
Ayurveda (AllAs) announced in the Union Budget 2026; and 
(d) the steps taken by the Government to strengthen research, education and healthcare 
infrastructure for the promotion and integration of Ayurveda through these initiatives?  
 
ANSWER 
THE MINISTER OF STATE (IC) OF THE MINISTRY OF AYUSH  
(SHRI PRATAPRAO JADHAV) 
 (a) to (d)  A Statement is laid on the table of the House. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

The Statement referred in reply to Lok Sabha Starred question no. 193 for 31.07.2026 
(a) & (b) The Ministry of Ayush is implementing a Central Sector Scheme namely 
Ayurgyan since 2021-22 with the aim to support Research & Innovation in Ayush by providing 
Extra Mural Research activities and Education by providing academic activities, training, 
Capacity Building etc.  The Scheme has 03 components viz. (i) Capacity Building & 
Continuing Medical Education (CME) in Ayush (ii) Research & Innovation (R&I) in Ayush 
from FY 2021-22 and (iii) Ayurveda Biology Integrated Health Research (ABIHR) was also 
added under the scheme as 3rd component in FY 2023-24. 
Being the  Central Sector Scheme, financial assistance is provided to the eligible 
institutions/organization across the country (including the state of Odisha) and the scheme is 
not specific to any State/UTs and regions .Under the Research & Innovation (R&I) in Ayus h 
and Ayurveda Biology Integrated Health Research (ABIHR) components of the Ayurgyan 
Scheme, 34 and 11 research projects were supported respectively since inception of the scheme 
(i.e. 2021-22) for a duration of three years and funds were released on insta lment basis. The 
details of the same is annexed at Annexure.  
The outcomes of the research projects are in the forms of product development, patents, 
technology developed, SOPs, presentations on international platform, publication in reputed 
journals etc. The anticipated outcomes are realized upon completion of the projects. A total 82 
research papers have been published in peer -reviewed journals under R&I component 
(including Erstwhile EMR) from FY 2021 -22 to as on 30.06.2026 . Further, under the R&I 
component of Ayurgyan Scheme, an amount of Rs.41.36 lakhs were relea sed to National 
Institute of Technology, Rourkela, located in the state of Odisha, for conducting the research 
project.  
(c) In pursuance of the announcement made in the recent Union Budget regarding the 
establishment of three new AIIAs, two committees namely, the Selection Committee and the 
Project Core Committee (PCC) have been constituted by the Ministry of Ayush for the purpose 
of site selection under the Challenge Method, issued by the Cabinet Secretariat. 
(d) To strengthen integration of Ayurveda with basic sciences and the conventional system of 
medicine through  high-end interdisciplinary  research by promoting  collaborative 
research between Ayush institutions  and institutions engaged in modern  biological scien ces, 
ABIHR component of Ayurgyan Scheme has been implemented from 2023-24. Further, under 
Centre of Excellence component of Ayurswasthya Yojana, there is a provision for financial 
assistance for upgradation of infrastructure and integrative research activities.  

 Ministry of Ayush is also implementing a Centrally Sponsored Scheme of National Ayush 
Mission (NAM) through State/UT Governments and supporting their efforts for overall 
development and promotion of Ayush systems of medicines including Ayurveda in the Country 
through State/UT Governments. The main objective of the scheme, inter-alia are as follows:  
➢ Co-location of Ayush facilities at Primary Health Centres (PHCs), Community Health 
Centres (CHCs) and District Hospitals (DHs). 
➢ Upgradation of existing standalone Government Ayush Hospitals. 
➢ Setting up of up to 10/30/50 bedded integrated Ayush Hospitals. 
➢ Establishment of new Ayush colleges in the States where availability of Ayush teaching 
institutions is inadequate in Government Sector. 
➢ Infrastructural development of Ayush Under -Graduate Institutions and Ayush Post -
Graduate Institutions/ add on PG/ Pharmacy /Para-Medical Courses. 
 Further, with regard to integration of Ayurveda, Government of India has adopted a 
strategy of Co -location of Ayush facilities at Primary Health Centres (PHCs),

(a) to (d) ‘Public Health’ & ‘Hospitals’ are State subjects. This Ministry provides technical and
financial support to the States/UTs including Maharashtra, for conducting screenings,
procurement of drugs for sickle cell anaemia and strengthening existing blood
banks/establishing new blood bank, based on the proposals received in the form of Programme
Implementation Plans (PIPs) under National Health Mission (NHM).
Under National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (NSCAEM), screenings in the
targeted age group of 0-40 years are conducted at all health facilities from District Hospitals
(DH) upto Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM) level in affected 17 tribal states including
Maharashtra for diagnosis of Sickle Cell Disease (SCD).
As reported by the States on SCD portal, as on 26.07.2026, more than 7.25 crore screenings
have been conducted in tribal dominated areas of the country including 1.11 crore in the State
of Maharashtra. As informed by State, number of persons screened, identified as carriers and
diagnosed with SCD in Gadchiroli, Chandrapur and Gondia district, under this Mission is at
Annexure.
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has devised the cost norms for establishment of Centres
of Excellence (CoE) on SCD funded by Ministry of Tribal Affairs (MoTA) in various states. 17
CoEs in 15 states including in AIIMS Nagpur, Maharashtra have been approved by MoTA.
Patients living with SCD are provided with counseling regarding lifestyle management,
pre-marriage and pre-natal decisions.
Hydroxyurea has been included in NHM Essential Drugs List at Sub-Health Centres, Primary
Health Centres (PHC)/ Urban PHC, Community Health Centres and DHs to address the issue
of access to medicine. To monitor the drug procurement and ensure the availability of essential
medicines in public health facilities, Drugs and Vaccine Distribution Management System
(DVDMS) has been launched by the Govt. of India.
Through MoTA, awareness and counseling material have been developed and shared with the
States for propagation of awareness of disease, screening and management.
Under Department of Health Research, ICMR has established the ICMR-National Institute for
Research in Tribal Health (NIRTH), Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh and a Centre for Research
Management and Control of Hemoglobinopathies in Chandrapur, Maharashtra which supports
national programs including sickle cell disease.

for students from remote, rural and aspirational districts, if so, the details thereof; 
(b) the number of learners enrolled through digital platforms under the initiative since its

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (A) TO (C) IN RESPECT OF LOK 
SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 2 ANSWERED ON 20.07.2026 REGARDING 
“NATIONAL DIGITAL UNIVERSITY INITIATIVE” ASKED BY SHRI BAIJAYANT 
PANDA, HON’BLE MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT 
 
(a) to (c): The Government of India has framed the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 with 
a vision to strengthen learner-centric and technology-enabled education. In alignment with this 
vision, the Government has envisaged the establishment of a Digital University platform to 
provide flexible and multidisciplinary learning. 
 
National Institute of Electronics & Information Technology (NIELIT), under the Ministry of 
Electronics & Information Technology (MeitY), has launched “NIELIT Digital University 
(NDU) Platform” in October 2025. NDU is a digital learning platform to deliver online and 
blended skill-based courses in emerging technology sectors such as Artificial Intelligence, 
Cybersecurity, Cloud Computing and other frontier domains. The courses on this digital 
platform are aligned to National Skill Qualification Framework (NSQF) with credits to be 
transferred in the Academic Bank of Credits (ABC) after successful completion. As on date, 
the NDU Platform host more than 100 courses, with over 2.70 Lakhs registration. 
 
Further, the Ministry of Education has undertaken several initiatives to strengthen the digital 
learning in higher education ecosystem. The University Grants Commission (UGC) Open & 
Distance Learning Programmes and Online Programmes Regulations, 2020 provide a 
framework for offering quality higher education through Open & Distance Learning and 
Online modes. In the Academic Year 2025-26, over 800 Online programmes were approved 
in more than 120 Universities/HEIs, with an enrolment of 4,26,196 learners.  
 
Further, premier institutions, including IITs, are offering online programmes in emerging areas 
such as Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, Machine Learning and Cyber Security. The online 
Bachelor of Science in Data Science programme by IIT Madras has seen more than 55000 
enrolments since 2021.    
 
Additionally, with a view to democratise quality education through digital technology, the 
Ministry of Education has initiated the SWAYAM online platform to provide free access to 
courses from premier institutions. There have been more than 20,000 deliveries of courses on 
the platform, with cumulative enrolments exceeding 6 crores since its inception. Further, under 
the UGC (Credit Framework for Online Learning Courses through SWAYAM) Regulations, 
2021, Higher Educational Institutions may offer up to 40% credits in a semester through 
SWAYAM. As of July 2026, 450 universities have adopted the SWAYAM framework for 
credit transfer.  
 
Further, to enhance industry-academia collaboration and improve employability of learners, 
the Ministry of Education has launched SWAYAM Plus platform. As of July 2026, the 
platform offers more than 500 industry-aligned courses across 15 sectors in collaboration with 
89 industry partners.

(a) to (c): Education is subject of concurrent list and both Central and State government 
work collaboratively to ensure comprehensive,  and progressive enhancement of overall 
quality and growth within the education sector.  Various schemes/ projects/ programmes run 
by the Ministry have been aligned with the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020. NEP 
2020 aims to ensure that no child loses o pportunity to learn and excel because of the 
circumstances of birth or background. It has taken into account the concerns of the Socio -
Economically Disadvantaged Groups (SEDGs) which inter -alia includes geographical 
identities such as students from village s, small towns, and aspirational districts and other 
categories. This policy aims at bridging the social category gaps in access, participation, and 
learning outcomes. 
 
The Ministry has launched the third phase of Rashtriya Uchchatar Shiksha Abhiyan (RUSA)  
as Pradhan Mantri Uchchatar Shiksha Abhiyan (PM -USHA) in June 2023 with an outlay of 
Rs. 12926.10 crore, including the committed liabilities of the earlier phases to cater to needs 
of educationally unserved/ underserved areas. The scheme has been further extended till 31 st 
March, 2028 for completion of PM -USHA projects and for additional 6 months (i.e till 30 th 
September, 2026) for completion of ongoing RUSA projects. It is a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme aimed at funding specific State government universities and colleges, including in 
the rural areas, so as to improve their quality by ensuring their conformity to  prescribed 
norms and standards. Under PM -USHA, priority is given to Focus Districts which are 
identified by the concerned States/ UTs based on various criteria including low Gross 
Enrolment Ratio, Gender Parity, population proportion and enrolment proportion for females, 
transgenders, Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and Other Backward Classes, 
Aspirational/ Border Area/ Left Wing Extremism prone district, etc. In particular, the Gender 
Inclusion and Equity Initiatives (GIEI) component of PM -USHA inter-alia also envisages to 
improve girls’ enrolment in higher education, particularly in focus districts, by promoting 
their greater participation in STEM, vocational and other professional courses. 
 
The Central Government has taken various measures to promote  higher education among the 
students across the nation including women, such as fee reductions, establishment of more 
institutes, scholarships, priority access to national level scholarships to aid students with poor 
financial backgrounds to pursue their education.  
 
University Grants Commission (UGC) is implementing scholarship scheme "National 
Scholarship for Post Graduate Studies (NSPG)" to provide scholarship to students pursuing 
Post Graduate Programs. UGC is also providing fellowships to pursue Ph.D. in all disciplines 
including STEM education, under UGC NET -Junior Research Fellowship and Savitribai 
Jyoti Rao Phule Single Girl Child Fellowship. 

 
Apart from this, UGC is implementing the scheme of “Development of Women’s Studies in 
Indian Universities and Colleges”. This scheme provides funds for setting up Women Studies 
Centers (WSCs) in universities and colleges, focusing on teaching, research, cu rriculum 
development, training and outreach activities. The objectives of the scheme are to provide 
financial support in advancing Women’s Studies through teaching, research and practical 
work. 
 
Similarly, All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) also offers various 
scholarships like AICTE Pragati Scholarship Scheme for Women (Degree & Diploma), 
AICTE PG scholarship Scheme, AICTE Doctoral Fellowship (ADF), AICTE Saksham 
Scholarship Scheme (Degree & Diploma) and AICTE Swanath Scholarship Scheme (Deg ree 
& Diploma). AICTE has also launched the AICTE Post -Docto

(a) to (e) Public Health & hospitals fall under the State list and therefore, the primary responsibility of
strengthening public healthcare system is with the States/Union Territories. However, under the National
Health Mission (NHM), the Government of India supports all States/Union Territories. States/Union
Territories submit their proposals through the annual Programme Implementation Plan (PIP), and based
on the available resource envelope (RE), the Government of India grants approvals in the Record of
Proceedings (RoPs) as per the approved norms and guidelines.
As updated by the States/Union Territories on Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM) portal, as on
30.06.2026, a total of 1,86,298 Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs) have been established and
operationalized in the country including 10,137 AAMs in Karnataka. The district-wise details of AAMs
in Karnataka is at Annexure-I.
